name: Delftware
summary: Tin-glazed earthenware that the potters of Delft made after 1640 to copy Chinese blue-and-white porcelain. A thin buff body takes a thick white tin glaze and cobalt painting in one firing.

philosophy.core_thesis: A cheap local clay looks like Chinese porcelain when a white tin glaze covers it and a fast brush paints it in cobalt blue.
design_principles: Cover the whole buff body with an opaque white tin glaze 0.5 to 1 mm thick.
Paint the cobalt on the raw, dry glaze in one pass; the glaze takes the stroke at once.
Divide a plate rim into 6 or 8 panels after Chinese kraak porcelain.
Put one scene in the well of the plate: a landscape, a flower vase or Chinese figures.
Give a fine piece a clear lead overglaze, the kwaart, for a higher gloss.
Fire the glaze at 1000 to 1100 °C in saggars, so that the flame does not touch the glaze.
Mark the base with the sign of the pottery and the initials of the owner.
anti_patterns: A translucent vitrified body that shows light through the wall
Thin even printed lines that repeat with no change of hand
A brown or red body left bare on the front face
Bright overglaze colours over the whole surface in the early work

form.shape: Flat plates and chargers with a wide rim, lobed dishes, tall vases and tulip vases with spouts, and jugs with a pewter lid.
form.profile: A shallow well that rises to a flat or slightly curved rim; vases have a round belly and a long neck after Chinese models.
form.foot_and_rim: A low foot ring or a flat base with holes for a hanging cord; the rim is plain or lobed, and the edge shows small chips of glaze.
form.proportion: Plate diameter 20 to 35 cm and wall 5 to 8 mm thick, which is thicker than the porcelain that it copies.
rules: Copy the shape of the Chinese model and keep the earthenware wall thicker.
Throw round ware on the wheel and press lobed dishes in moulds.
Keep the back of a plate glazed white, often with a thinner lead glaze.

bodies.rule: Mix three local and imported marls into a buff earthenware that fires soft and takes a thick tin glaze. Keep porcelain out: delftware copies it.

methods: press moulding in plaster or clay moulds
forming.joins: Handles and spouts are pulled or moulded and luted with slip; metal lids are mounted after the firing.
forming.details: Three small marks of the kiln stilts under the rim, a slightly uneven glaze edge, and a pottery mark painted under the base.

glaze.pattern: Chinese landscapes, flower vases, birds on branches, Dutch windmills and biblical scenes in cobalt blue on white, in panels after kraak porcelain.
glaze.gloss: Satin to gloss, about 40 to 70 GU; pieces with a kwaart overglaze are brighter.
glaze.wear: The tin glaze chips at the rim and shows the buff body under it; the colour of the painting stays fresh.

palette.strategy: Cobalt blue on a milk-white ground; after 1700 some pieces add manganese purple, iron red and a little gold.

firing.kiln: A wood-fired updraught kiln with saggars; one firing for the biscuit and one for the glaze.
firing.scale: Some 30 potteries in Delft in the 1660s to 1720s, each with tens of painters on piece work.
firing.signs: A pottery mark under the base, stilt marks on the back, and a slight blue blur where the cobalt sank into the glaze.

pieces.form: Plate with a flat rim in 8 panels and a Chinese landscape in the well
Lobed oval dish pressed in a mould, with a flower vase in the centre
Deep bowl with Chinese figures in a garden round the outside
Small plate with a polychrome flower basket and a gilt rim

positive: still-life museum photograph, soft north light

Tile picture of a flower vase

emotion.target_response: A quiet, homely calm: the viewer sees a free blue brush on a clean white ground and thinks of a Dutch kitchen or a cabinet of porcelain.

triggers: blue and white tiles and plates
use_cases: a tableware pattern brief in Dutch blue and white
a still-life or interior prompt with period plates
a museum label on Dutch tin-glazed earthenware
avoid_when: the brief wants an industrial printed pattern
the brief is for oven or dishwasher ware

modifiers.how: Change the body to porcelain, keep the panelled rim, and fire to about 1300 °C.
Change to a white earthenware with a clear glaze and print the blue pattern from a copper plate.

wall_thickness.note: Earthenware plates are thicker than the porcelain that they copy.
